quiz.title: Chapter 7 Quiz: Regulations and Administrative Research
quiz.intro: Ten questions on how a rule is made, which publication holds which answer, and how to confirm a regulation is current.

items.q: Regulations carry the force of law when:
options: An agency posts them on its website
They are properly adopted under authority a statute delegated, typically through APA notice-and-comment
They appear in a guidance document
items.why: A regulation is valid only if it falls within the scope of its authorizing statute (How Regulations Are Made).

items.q: Which publication is the daily record of proposed rules, final rules, and notices?
items.why: The CFR is the annual codification of effective rules; the Federal Register records the rulemaking (Organization of Federal Regulatory Publications).

items.q: The chapter calls the final rule’s preamble:
options: Often your single best interpretive resource, the regulatory equivalent of legislative history
items.why: Stopping at the CFR text without the preamble is the most common regulatory research error (How Regulations Are Made; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: The authority note at the start of a CFR part tells you:
options: When the part was last amended
Which statute empowers the agency to issue the part
items.why: The source note, by contrast, cites the Federal Register document that created or last amended the part (Organization of Federal Regulatory Publications).

items.q: The most current freely available version of a regulation is in:
items.why: Each eCFR title carries a note showing the date through which it is updated (Answering Questions with Regulations and Updating for Currency).

items.q: The List of CFR Sections Affected (LSA) is used to:
options: Find a regulation by popular name
Catch intervening amendments when working from the annual CFR edition
items.why: Agencies revise regulations far more often than legislatures amend statutes, so currency matters even more here (Updating for Currency).

items.q: Which question is a regulation the primary tool for?
options: I have a workplace safety problem; where do I start?
What specific requirements must a food manufacturer meet to label a product organic?
Who was the first EPA administrator?
How do I draft a complaint?
items.why: Regulations answer focusing questions about how a statutory mandate operates and definitional questions about terms delegated to agencies (Questions This Source Answers).

items.q: If you already hold a CFR citation, the chapter says to:
options: Retrieve it directly in the eCFR and skip the search
items.why: Retrieve, don’t search, the same rule as Chapter 2 (Searching for Regulations).

items.q: A guidance document that has not gone through notice-and-comment:
options: Lacks the force of law but is highly influential as a statement of how the agency interprets and enforces its rules
items.why: Treating guidance as a binding regulation can lead you to tell a client something is required when it is only the agency’s preference (Guidance Documents; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: For state regulations, the research process:
options: Has no equivalent to the federal model
Mirrors the federal model: locate the authorizing statute, find the implementing regulation, check for updates
Always starts in the Federal Register
items.why: State registers publish proposed and final rules; state codes compile them by subject (State Administrative Materials).

drills.title: Which Publication?
drills.blurb: Federal regulations move through a fixed set of publications. Match each need to the one that answers it.

drills.title: The Life of a Rule
drills.blurb: From the statute that authorized it to the day you check it is still current. Put the stages in order.
